title: Overview of Red Meat Slaughter and Dress Procedures

lessons.title: Lairage, stunning and bleeding
lessons.html:
Receiving and lairage

Animals are offloaded calmly using ramps at the right height, checked against movement documents, and placed in pens by owner. They are inspected ante-mortem and given water. Rest reduces stress, which improves meat quality. Injured animals are given priority for slaughter so they do not suffer. All handling must comply with the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962.

Stunning

Stunning makes the animal immediately unconscious so that it feels no pain during bleeding.

SpeciesCommon methodSigns of effective stun
CattlePenetrating captive bolt to the forehead, in a stunning box or restrainerImmediate collapse, no rhythmic breathing, no eye (corneal) reflex, relaxed jaw and tongue
Sheep and goatsElectrical head-only stunning with tongs, or captive boltRigid phase followed by paddling, no rhythmic breathing, no eye reflex
PigsElectrical stunning, or gas stunning in some large plantsAs for sheep; no righting reflex

Captive bolt guns must be cleaned, maintained and test-fired according to the manufacturer and abattoir procedure. Electrical stunners need correct settings and clean electrodes. A spare stunner must be ready. If any animal shows signs of regaining consciousness, re-stun immediately.

Safety: captive bolt guns are dangerous tools. Only trained, authorised operators may use them. Never point one at a person. Unload and store them safely.

Bleeding (sticking)

Bleeding must follow stunning quickly, within the time set in your procedures, so the animal does not regain consciousness. Cattle are usually stuck in the chest to cut the major vessels near the heart; sheep and pigs by a neck or chest stick. Use a clean, sterilised knife, and for cattle a second knife for the stick. Good bleeding improves carcass appearance and shelf life.

lessons.title: Dressing cattle and small stock
lessons.html:
Dressing: removing head, feet and hide

Dressing is where most carcass contamination happens. The principle is to keep the outside of the hide away from the meat.

Typical cattle dressing sequence

  1. Remove the head after bleeding, keeping it identified with the carcass for inspection.
  2. Remove front and hind feet.
  3. Open the hide along set lines using the inside-out cutting technique so hair does not touch meat.
  4. Flay the legs, brisket and flanks by hand.
  5. Rod the oesophagus (tie or clip it) to stop rumen content leaking.
  6. Free and bag the bung (rectum).
  7. Pull the hide off using a hide puller where available, controlling the pull so the hide does not flap onto the carcass.

Small stock

Sheep and goats are often dressed on a line using fisting (pushing the skin off by hand) to reduce knife use and contamination. Avoid contact between wool and meat. The pelt is removed downwards and away from the carcass. Workers who touch the pelt must wash hands before touching meat.

Evisceration

  1. Open the belly carefully without cutting the stomachs or intestines.
  2. Remove the green offal (stomachs and intestines) into a clean tray or chute.
  3. Cut through the diaphragm and remove the red offal (lungs, heart, liver) as a set or pluck.
  4. Keep offal identified with the carcass for inspection.

If gut content spills, stop, inform the supervisor and the inspector, and trim the contaminated area.

Splitting

Cattle carcasses are split along the middle of the backbone with a saw that is sterilised between carcasses. Accurate splitting avoids exposing spinal cord to contamination and keeps both sides of equal value.

lessons.title: Pig dressing, final steps and supervision
lessons.html:
Pigs: scalding and dehairing

After bleeding, pigs are usually scalded in hot water to loosen the hair, then dehaired by machine and by hand scraping. Some plants singe the skin to remove remaining hair. Watch for:

  • Water temperature and time in the scald tank, set by procedure; too hot cooks the skin, too cold leaves hair.
  • Pigs not fully dead before scalding: this is a serious welfare offence. Bleeding must be complete first.
  • Scald water entering the lungs, which leads to condemnation of the lungs.
  • Dirty scald water; it must be changed and the tank cleaned as scheduled.

Evisceration and splitting of pigs follow similar principles to cattle.

Final carcass steps

  1. Post-mortem inspection of head, offal and carcass by the meat inspector.
  2. Trimming of contamination, bruises and inspection trims.
  3. Washing to remove bone dust and blood, not to remove faecal contamination.
  4. Weighing on calibrated scales; the hot carcass mass is recorded.
  5. Classification by a registered classifier and roller marking.
  6. Inspection marking of passed carcasses.
  7. Chilling.

What the foreman watches

  • Stunning effectiveness and the time from stunning to bleeding.
  • Knife sterilising and hand washing at every station.
  • Hide and pelt control, rodding and bagging.
  • Cut guts and contamination rates.
  • Line balance and worker safety at saws and hide pullers.

Key points

  • Stunning must make the animal unconscious immediately; re-stun if signs of consciousness appear.
  • Bleed quickly after stunning with a clean knife.
  • Use inside-out cutting and keep hide or wool away from meat.
  • Rod the oesophagus and bag the bung before evisceration.
  • Pigs must be fully bled and dead before scalding.

quiz.question: Which is a sign of effective stunning in cattle?

options.text: Immediate collapse and no eye reflex

quiz.question: Why must bleeding follow stunning quickly?

options.text: So the animal does not regain consciousness
So the hide comes off more easily

quiz.question: What is fisting in small stock dressing?

options.text: Pushing the skin off by hand to reduce knife use

quiz.question: Why is the oesophagus rodded (tied or clipped)?

options.text: To stop rumen content leaking onto the carcass

quiz.question: What is carcass washing used for?

options.text: Cooling the carcass to dispatch temperature

quiz.question: A pig may be put into the scald tank before bleeding is complete if the line is busy.
Only trained, authorised operators may use a captive bolt gun.
Which steps help prevent contamination during dressing? (select all that apply)

options.text: Letting the hide flap onto the carcass
Washing hands after touching the pelt
